name: Bell Labs 128-by-106 frame-transfer CCD area imager
description: Bell Labs built a two-dimensional CCD array that electronically scanned a whole image. In frame-transfer mode it moved the captured charge pattern into a shielded storage region, then shifted each row into a serial register for readout. In a separate mode the team also used the full 128-by-106 array for slower imaging.

date.basis: Date of the NASA Headquarters symposium, documented in the proceedings.

events.statement: Carlo H. Séquin presented the working Bell Labs area CCD and showed a picture produced with the device at 15 frames per second.

evidence.locator: Title page and preface; pp. 57–61, Figures IV-8–10
evidence.supports: Dates the presentation, describes the architecture and identifies the reproduced image and its operating conditions.

events.caveats: The date is that of the presentation. The proceedings were published in 1973.

date.basis: Issue date of IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices 20(3).

events.statement: The Bell Labs team published images from the 64-by-106 sensing region in frame-transfer mode and from all 128-by-106 elements in a slower mode.

evidence.locator: pp. 244 and 247–248, abstract, Results and Figure 4
evidence.supports: The images, separate modes and readout conditions are reported by the experimenters.

earliest_record.rationale: The dated symposium presentation describes the working array and documents an image.

links.statement: The area imager implemented the frame-transfer geometry outlined in the 96-element line-imager report. It combined a two-dimensional integration array, a shielded store and a serial output register.
links.caveats: The cited design is the area-imager proposal in the 1971 line-imager paper. This relationship concerns that design and its later implementation.

evidence.supports: The line-imager researchers diagram a possible three-phase area imager with integration, shielded storage and serial readout.
Séquin illustrates the working layout, including the serial readout, and cites the 1971 line-imager paper.
The working array’s authors explicitly credit their frame-transfer principle to the line-imager report and document the implemented geometry.
Independent RCA engineers describe those same three functional regions and cite Bell’s 1971 and 1972 imaging papers.
